identification: Framed vintage photograph of Eskleigh homestead, Perth (Tasmania, near Launceston), 13x19 cm

story: Eskleigh was built in 1870 as 'Scone' for William Gibson junior (architect Harry Conway), a two-storey 18-room house above the South Esk River at Perth. In 1944 Gibson gave it as a home for permanently incapacitated people (the Home of Peace), renamed Eskleigh, and it still operates as a care and respite home; it also has an art collection shown at QVMAG. https://historyoverdinner.com/eskleigh-perth-home-of-peace/

identification: Lot of used early Australian stamps in stock books: Kangaroo and Map issues and many used KGV heads (per brief; pre-existing pricing of A$25 at Gowans Hobart Dec 2025 and Jan 2026 not re-verified by me)

story: The Kangaroo and Map stamps were the Commonwealth's first national postage stamps, released 2 January 1913 after a 1911 design competition, and were widely criticised in the press at the time (Professor Tucker in The Argus called it 'Making a nation ridiculous'). Used Kangaroos and KGV heads remain a classic starter collecting area, with high denominations the valuable ones. https://www.australianculture.org/kangaroo-and-map-stamps/

story: The thylacine (Tasmanian tiger) was hunted out under a government bounty scheme and the last known captive animal died at Hobart's Beaumaris Zoo in September 1936; painted souvenir trays and boards like this are part of the long Tasmanian tourist trade in thylacine imagery. No record of the named artist found. Source for general thylacine background: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thylacine (not fetched; background knowledge only).

identification: Small oil painting 'King River Tasmania' by Janet Morley, 16 x 21 cm
viewing_check: Check for signature and whether it is oil on board; subject is the King River, West Coast Tasmania.

story: The King River runs 52 km from the West Coast Range to Macquarie Harbour near Strahan and was once called Australia's most polluted river: from the 1880s the Mount Lyell copper mine at Queenstown dumped waste and, from 1922 to 1995, about 1.5 million tonnes of tailings a year into the Queen/King system, building a delta of around 100 million tonnes in the harbour. Its upper valley was drowned by the Crotty Dam (Lake Burbury) in 1992, and the old Abt rack railway ran along the lower river. Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/King_River_(Tasmania)

story: The 1797 'cartwheel' penny was struck by Matthew Boulton's Soho Mint in Birmingham, the first steam-powered coinage, and was a full ounce of copper with a heavy raised rim, hence the name; Noble Numismatics describes the Soho Mint issues in their George III copper lots. identification: Six British George VI .500 silver coins in holders: halfcrowns (1946 marked UNC, two others EF) and two-shilling florins (1937, 1938, 1946), as annotated on the holders
viewing_check: Check the dates and grades on the holders against the coins; 1946 is the last year of 50% silver, and any scratches or cleaning matter.
searches_tried: WebSearch x2: George VI half crown/florin silver content and value; 1946 half crown EF value. Noble Numismatics lot 850, sale 80 shows a 1946 halfcrown EF-nearly UNC realised $100 (estimate $60), but the page gives no sale date so it is not entered. coincraft.com has a Cloudflare bot check, skipped. bullionbypost spot silver on 6 Nov 2026 was US$51.91/oz, but no per-coin price seen.
story: Britain debased its silver coinage from 92.5% to 50% silver in 1920 (halfcrown mass 14.14 g), and stopped silver coins altogether in 1947 when cupronickel replaced them, so these 1937-1946 pieces are the last of the silver halfcrowns and florins. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_crown_(British_coin)

identification: Taxidermy hazel grouse (Tetrastes bonasia), a Eurasian woodland gamebird, mounted on a driftwood base, about 26 cm high
viewing_check: Hazel grouse do not occur in Australia, so this is an imported or old European mount. Check for a taxidermist or dealer label, moth or feather damage, and ask about import paperwork if you plan to resell or export it.
searches_tried: WebSearch x3: taxidermy hazel grouse mount sold auction; hazel grouse facts; hazel grouse taxidermy for sale price. Burstow & Hewett lot opened turned out to be a puffin (GBP 130 hammer), not comparable, not recorded. No hazel grouse price found.
story: The hazel grouse was formally described by Linnaeus in 1758 and lives in dense forests across Europe and Asia; early 20th century English travellers to Russia called it the 'rabchick'. This mount is a long way from home, as the bird is not found in Australia. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hazel_grouse

viewing_check: Identify each coin and wreck (VOC Zuytdorp/Vergulde Draeck/Batavia silver, Admiral Gardiner, 1715 Plate Fleet cobs etc.) and look for certificates of authenticity and Australian legality paperwork. Some Australian wreck coins are protected finds that must be documented; copies or 'souvenir' sets are common.
searches_tried: WebSearch: shipwreck coins Tasmania/VOC Zuytdorp; shipwreck coins collection sold auction Australia. Fetched Noble lot 383042 (wrong item), Treasures Auctions 50294 (limited edition 1808 Admiral Gardiner + two 1715 cobs, closed 14 Sep 2025, only a 1 AUD bid shown, no clear result so not used), Sterling Currency Zuytdorp article. story: The VOC ship Zuytdorp left the Netherlands in 1711 and was wrecked on the Western Australian coast in June 1712; it was not found until 1964, and its entire 1711 Zeeland mintage of silver 6 stuiver coins went down with it. Only a few hundred wreck coins are legally held privately (616 reported), which is why provenance matters. Source: https://sterlingcurrency.com.au/blog/news-research/commonwealth-coins/the-silver-coins-of-the-zuytdorp-shipwreck (only relevant if the Armitage coins are from that wreck, which is unconfirmed).

viewing_check: Check dents and enamel losses, whether the base and rim are brass or copper-gilt, any marks on the base, and whether the filigree wire is fine (older) or coarse and machine-like (later export).
searches_tried: WebSearch: pair Chinese cloisonne vases 17 cm sold auction; cloisonne history China. Read Gorringes lot (sold 3 Oct 2023) and Regent Antiques (asking). Both only partial matches.
story: Cloisonne reached China via the Silk Road in the Yuan dynasty and became an imperial art by the 15th century (the 'Jingtai blue' period); under Qianlong in the 18th century the wirework became finer and more painterly, and many later 19th-century pieces carry apocryphal reign marks, so a small dented pair is more likely later export ware than palace quality. Source: https://nwtiques.com/blogs/blog/the-history-of-chinese-cloisonne-enamel
